work.text: In my figures … I have achieved a great simplicity, which is both rustic and superstitious … In this picture the landscape and the struggle … exist only in the imagination of the people whom the sermon has moved to prayer.

work.text: Following Bernard's example but developing it further, Gauguin painted Vision After the Sermon, which marked his interest in interpreting religious subject matter in a highly personal way. He became recognized as the leader of a new style called Synthetism.

moment.text: Far, very far away on a mysterious little hill-top, whose soil is of shining vermilion, is the biblical struggle of Jacob and the Angel.

source.author: G.-Albert Aurier
source.title: Article on Gauguin in the Mercure de France, quoted in The Letters of Paul Gauguin to Georges Daniel de Monfreid, trans. Ruth Pielkovo (1922)

moment.text: Finding inspiration in Japanese woodblock prints from Hiroshige and Hokusai, which he owned, Gauguin developed the idea of non-naturalistic landscapes. He applies large areas of flat color to the composition, and the red ground departs from the conventional representation of earth, field, or grass.

What I dislike is that he copied these elements from the Japanese, the Byzantine painters and others. I criticize him for not applying his synthesis to our modern philosophy which is absolutely social, anti-authoritarian
moment.lead: His old mentor Camille Pissarro was not persuaded:

matters.text: I love Brittany; I find wildness and primitiveness there. When my wooden shoes ring on this granite, I hear the muffled, dull, and powerful tone which I try to achieve in painting.

source.author: Paul Gauguin
source.title: Letter to a friend, in The Writings of a Savage, ed. Daniel Guérin, trans. Eleanor Levieux (1996), p. 109, quoted on Wikiquote
source.license: Short excerpt of an English translation, via Wikiquote (CC BY-SA)

matters.text: In the early part of his career as a painter, Gauguin had painted primarily landscapes en plein air in the Impressionist manner. By 1888, he had become dissatisfied with Impressionism, which did not satisfy his enthusiasm for archaic and primitive forms or his interest in the mystical.
